chapter: Discovering Henderson, clarinet and first gigs
title: Summer roadhouse job near Albany with Jimmy Campbell
summary: He played a Prohibition-era gangster roadhouse in Albany in a small band with drummer Jimmy Campbell, later joined by Johnny Russell, and learned from the older pianist Paddy Armstead.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Now, what about Campbell, the drummer, Jimmy Campbell. Was that --

Yes, Jimmy Campbell. He was a fellow out of Brooklyn. He was a drummer, and I don't remember just how I got in contact with him. But it was a summer job, up in Albany, at this roadhouse. You know, they used to call them roadhouses in those days. They were out of town and of course this was during prohibition, and they sold bootleg whiskey and the gangsters. I think it was -- it was a gangster house, of course it was. I remember the fellow who owned it was an old Irishman named Ames O'Brien, yeah, and so we played up there with him. We had how many pieces? A drummer, a piano player, a
guitar player and myself, four pieces. Yeah. Then later on, we added another piece. We added Johnny Russell. Did you ever hear of Johnny Russell, a tenor player?
Then we got him and he came up there and played.
Now, was this still playing stock arrangements?

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, we -- that's what it was. We had a -- and the piano player, what was his name? His name was Paddy somebody. He was an elderly fellow. Oh, I don't know if I should say older fellow, because he'd been playing, you know, professionally around New York for quite awhile, and he -- you know, he sort of had control of the band and he -- in other words the kind of fellow you could learn a lot from and I learned a lot from him and he could play those charts good, you know, and tell you, you know, this goes like that, you know, and all that sort of thing.
Paddy Armstead, his name was, yeah.
